nameStory: The threeline mudsnail gets its name from the three distinctive dark spiral lines that wrap around its shell like tiny racing stripes. These lines are so characteristic that early naturalists used them as the defining feature to distinguish this species from its plainer cousins. The scientific name 'trivittata' literally means 'three-striped' in Latin, making this one of those happy cases where the common and scientific names tell the same story.
description: The threeline mudsnail is a small marine snail that crawls through the muddy shallows of New England's salt marshes and tidal flats. Its conical shell is typically grayish-brown with three prominent dark spiral bands that circle the shell from top to bottom. These hardy little snails are scavengers, using their keen sense of smell to locate dead fish, clams, and other organic matter in the mud. They're an essential part of the coastal cleanup crew, helping to recycle nutrients in these productive ecosystems.

idTips.label: Three dark spiral lines
idTips.description: Look for three distinct dark brown or black lines that spiral around the shell from the pointed tip to the opening - these are the snail's signature feature and are usually clearly visible even on weathered shells

idTips.label: Shell shape and size
idTips.description: The shell feels sturdy and conical in your hand, typically about the size of your thumbnail, with a pointed spire that tapers to a sharp tip

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell surface feels slightly rough with fine growth lines and may have a chalky or worn appearance from tumbling in the surf and sand

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Base shell color ranges from light gray to brownish, but those three dark spiral bands stand out clearly against the lighter background

idTips.label: Opening characteristics
idTips.description: The shell opening (aperture) is oval-shaped with a smooth inner lip that often appears white or cream-colored

habitat: Look for threeline mudsnails in the muddy or sandy bottoms of salt marshes, tidal creeks, and protected bays throughout coastal New England. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can easily burrow and are often found mixed with clam shells and eelgrass beds. You'll have the best luck finding them during low tide when they're exposed on mudflats or in shallow tide pools.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge from deeper waters as temperatures warm, making this a good time to find live specimens crawling through shallow tide pools and marsh edges.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most active and easiest to observe feeding and moving across mudflats during low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper water; shells of deceased individuals often wash up on beaches during autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Live snails retreat to deeper waters, but empty shells can still be found mixed in with other beach wrack and shell collections.

funFact: Threeline mudsnails are like underwater bloodhounds - they can smell a dead fish from over 30 feet away and will form feeding frenzies around carcasses, with dozens of snails converging on a single food source like tiny aquatic vultures.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Eastern Mudsnail, which lacks the three distinctive spiral lines and has a more uniformly colored shell. Memory trick: 'Three lines, threeline' - if you can count three distinct dark bands spiraling around the shell, you've got your threeline mudsnail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mudsnails,' these creatures are actually quite clean and play an important ecological role as nature's recyclers in coastal environments. The Nassariidae family they belong to is sometimes called 'dog whelks,' though this name is more commonly applied to other marine snail families.
compareHints: The threeline mudsnail is easily distinguished from its close relative, the Eastern Mudsnail, by those characteristic three dark spiral bands - Eastern Mudsnails have a more uniform coloration without distinct banding. While both species live in similar muddy habitats, only the threeline mudsnail sports those racing stripe-like markings that make identification straightforward.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern mudsnails are generally larger and more uniformly dark than their close relative, the threeline mudsnail (Ilyanassa trivittata).
